label: inadequate hood coverage
description:
A directly visible grease/smoke-producing appliance with visibly inadequate hood coverage, subject to the evidence requirements below. Eligible appliances include fryers, griddles, charbroilers, open ranges, woks, salamanders/broilers, and conveyor pizza ovens. Never infer an appliance from a suppression system, tank, pipe, or service tag.
Wall- or table-mounted broilers/salamanders qualify as grease-producing appliances requiring a hood; do not dismiss them as conveyor toasters. Countertop/low-grease units such as conveyor toasters, microwaves, food warmers, steam kettles, and dishwashers do not qualify.
Check every grease-producing appliance, including portable units on side tables, items at the far left/right of the line, and anything in a gap between two hoods.
A hood is an overhead canopy with a grease-filter bank. The following are NOT hoods and do not provide coverage: a wire rack, an open wall shelf, a salamander/storage shelf, or any shelving above an appliance. A grease appliance sitting under only a shelf or rack lacks coverage.
Apply this label only with positive proof of at least one of the following:
- The ceiling directly above the appliance is visible, and the full gap between the appliance and ceiling is clearly free of any hood. Seeing the ceiling or a wall above an appliance is NOT by itself proof of a missing hood, because a hood frequently mounts to the side or extends out of frame. Only conclude "no hood" when the appliance's entire overhead envelope—including every side where a hood could attach—is visible in-frame and unobstructed.
- The hood's physical front or side edge—not the photo border—is visible, and the appliance clearly continues past it. Do not treat a hood's end skirt, triangular end, or side canopy panel as the terminal filter edge. To judge whether an appliance is past the canopy, check what it backs onto: an appliance set against a plain wall, backsplash, or a vertical pipe—rather than the hood's own backsplash—is outside the footprint.
Do not apply this label if the hood, the space above the appliance, or the ceiling is cut off, out of frame, blurred, or otherwise unconfirmable. A tight crop alone does not establish inadequate coverage. Do not apply this label when steep angles or perspective distortion make it ambiguous whether the appliance extends past the hood's edge.
Appliances with their own integral/attached hood, filter unit, or ventless recirculating ventilation are adequately covered—do not apply this label to them.
When the proof requirements are met, apply this label if the appliance is outside the Type I hood footprint, under a Type II/non-grease vent, or lacks approximately 6 inches of overhang. Type I hoods have vertical slatted metal grease baffles; Type II hoods show wire mesh, honeycomb, or flat plates (and often no fire-suppression nozzle) and serve heat/steam applications rather than grease-producing appliances. A Type II vent directly over a grease-producing appliance (e.g., a fryer or range) is inadequate coverage—apply the label.
In the classification explanation, cite the ceiling, hood-edge, shelf/rack, or Type II filter evidence.

label: hood missing filter
description:
A commercial exhaust hood with an entire filter panel absent, leaving a panel-sized opening with the empty rack or plenum visible behind it. A panel missing at an end of the bank, or a bank that is entirely empty, both qualify — acceptable in shadow if the empty rack itself is clearly visible.
Do NOT apply for: an opening beside a filter that is still installed, or a slanted/dislodged/damaged filter (those are bypass gaps); a solid blanking panel; a self-cleaning/water-wash filter's designed top opening; the inner canopy end or plenum where no filter belongs; or darkness alone with no visible empty rack.

label: hood grease buildup
description:
A visible grease deposit on an interior hood surface: filter faces, baffle-channel interiors, or the rails/trough above or below the filters. Thickness is not required — a thin deposit counts.
Apply when an interior surface shows deposited grease, such as: yellow, orange, or brown grease discoloration or staining; a tacky, filmy, or textured coating in patches or streaks; dripping, pooling, or drip trails along or below the rails; or raised, crusted, caked, or burnt-looking grease.
Do NOT apply for: a thin uniform light film from normal use; plain metal aging; reflections, shadows, soot, rust, water or condensation, or cleaning marks; grease in a collection cup or trough working as designed; or grease on exterior canopy faces, walls, or backsplashes.

label: fryer missing baffle
description:
A deep-fat fryer beside an open-flame appliance without an adequate separating baffle, with all of the following clearly visible:
1. A deep-fat fryer with a visible oil vat and fry basket(s) beside an open-flame appliance. The open-flame appliance is identified by exposed flame or open burner grates; an open-burner range and a wok burner both qualify as flame sources. A flat-top griddle, enclosed oven, salamander, and other fryers do NOT qualify as the flame source. A fry basket resting on a table, counter, or inside a wok is NOT a fryer; identify the fryer by its own oil vat, not by a loose basket.
2. Both the edge of the fryer and the edge of the adjacent flame appliance, and the full gap between them, must be clearly visible. If either appliance's edge is out of frame or occluded, do not apply this label—you cannot confirm the absence of a baffle you cannot see.
3. The appliances are directly adjacent, approximately 16 inches or less apart, with no appliance, table, or object between them. If any appliance or object (e.g., a side table, a griddle, a bucket) sits between the fryer and the flame source, they are not directly adjacent.
4. The intervening gap has no solid steel or tempered-glass baffle approximately 8 inches or taller, or the baffle is clearly too short or misplaced to separate the fryer from the open-flame appliance.
Inspect the gap between the appliances directly. A baffle may be thin and hard to see from a head-on angle—do not conclude "no baffle" unless the gap is clearly visible and you can positively confirm the absence of any divider. Rear walls and backsplashes do not count as separating baffles. Do not assume fryer width equals 16 inches; estimate the separation from visible cues and state your basis. In side or oblique views, perspective distorts apparent distance—if the viewing angle makes the separation or the presence of a baffle unreliable to judge, do not apply this label.
Do not apply this label if a qualifying baffle is present, separation exceeds approximately 16 inches, the flame source is actually a griddle or other non-flame appliance, a loose basket (not a fryer vat) is the only "fryer" present, or the appliance edges/gap are out of frame, occluded, or at an angle too steep to confirm any required condition.

label: hood bypass gap
description:
An opening around a still-installed filter that exposes the space behind the filter plane, letting air bypass the media. A whole missing panel is a missing filter, not a bypass gap. These gaps are often small and subtle — inspect carefully and do not default to 'properly seated.'
Apply when such an opening is visible, even a small one, at any of: the seam between two adjacent panels (including at or beside the handles); between an end panel and the hood's side frame or wall; along a filter's top or bottom edge at the rail; or at a tilted, bowed, recessed, protruding, dislodged, bent, or damaged filter or baffle channel.
Do NOT apply for: the normal vertical baffle channels inside a single intact filter; a flush seam between properly seated panels with no space visible behind it; reflections, highlights, dark bands, or colored shapes on the filter face; handles, frame rails, or grease staining by themselves; or an entirely empty slot (missing filter).
